Pues, mientras renqueaba arriba, quejándome de mis débiles tobillos con la ronca y mascullante voz que había asumido, contemplé un pedacito de ella, echando apenas un ojo, con la puerta entornada, para observar quién subía; y, viendo a tan viejo y torpe sujeto con gabán en tiempo tan cálido, calado y arrebujado, se retiró, cerrando la puerta sin emoción alguna. Mas no fue así conmigo; pues no puedes imaginar cómo me danzó el corazón hasta la boca al solo vislumbre de ella, de suerte que temí que el villano que golpea, golpea, golpea, el cual tan recientemente había golpeado otro tanto sin propósito, me ahogara.

I saw!---I saw, she was! for as I hobbled up, crying out upon my weak ankles in the hoarse mumbling voice I had assumed, I beheld a little piece of her, just casting an eye, with the door ajar, as they call it, to observe who was coming up; and, seeing such an old clumsy fellow great-coated in weather so warm, slouched and muffled up, she withdrew, shutting the door without any emotion. But it was not so with me; for thou canst not imagine how my heart danced to my mouth at the very glimpse of her; so that I was afraid the thump, thump, thumping villain, which had so lately thumped as much to no purpose, would have choked me.

Me gustaron mucho los alojamientos, y tanto más cuanto que dijo que el tercer aposento era aún más hermoso.

I liked the lodgings well; and the more, as she said the third room was still handsomer. I must sit down, madam (and chose the darkest part of the room). Won't you take a seat yourself? No price shall part us. But I will leave the terms to you and my wife, if you please: and also whether for board or not. Only please to take this for earnest, putting a guinea into her hand---And one thing I will say; my poor wife loves money; but is not an ill-natured woman. She was a great fortune to me: but, as the real estate goes away at her death, I would fain preserve her for that reason, as well as for the love I bear her as an honest man. But if she makes too close a bargain with you, tell me; and, unknown to her, I will make it up. This is my constant way: she loves to have her pen'worths; and I would not have her vexed or made uneasy on any account.

—He de sentarme, señora (y escogí la parte más oscura del cuarto). ¿No queréis tomar asiento vos también? Ningún precio nos separará. Mas dejaré los términos a vos y a mi esposa, si os place; y también si ha de ser con pensión o no. Sólo tened a bien tomar esto como señal (poniéndole una guinea en la mano). Y una cosa diré: mi pobre esposa ama el dinero, mas no es mujer de mal natural. Fue gran fortuna para mí; mas, como la hacienda raíz se va a su muerte, de buena gana la preservaría por esa razón, así como por el amor que le tengo como hombre honrado. Mas, si hiciera con vos trato demasiado cerrado, decídmelo a mí; y, sin que ella lo sepa, os lo compensaré. Este es mi constante modo: le gusta que le cundan sus cuartos, y yo no querría verla vejada ni inquieta por cuenta alguna.

She said I was a very considerate gentleman; and, upon the condition I had mentioned, she was content to leave the terms to my lady.

Dijo que era yo caballero muy considerado, y que, con la condición que había mencionado, se contentaba con dejar los términos a mi dama.

But, madam, cannot a body just peep into the other apartment, that I may be more particular to my wife in the furniture of it?

—Mas, señora, ¿no puede uno asomarse al otro aposento, para poder ser más particular con mi esposa acerca de su moblaje?

The lady desires to be private, sir---but---and was going to ask her leave.

—La dama desea estar privada, señor. Mas... —y se disponía a pedirle licencia.

I caught hold of her hand---However, stay, stay, madam: it mayn't be proper, if the lady loves to be private. Don't let me intrude upon the lady---

Le así la mano.

No intrusion, sir, I dare say: the lady is good-humoured. She will be so kind as to step down into the parlour, I dare say. As she stays so little a while, I am sure she will not wish to stand in my way.

—Con todo, alto, alto, señora: puede no ser propio, si la dama ama lo privado. No dejéis que yo me entrometa con la dama.

No, madam, that's true, if she be good-humoured, as you say---Has she been with you long, madam?

—Ninguna intrusión, señor, me atrevo a decir: la dama es de buen humor. Tendrá la bondad de bajar a la salita, no lo dudo. Como está aquí tan poco tiempo, estoy segura de que no deseará estorbarme.

But yesterday, sir---

—No, señora; eso es cierto, si es de buen humor, como decís. ¿Lleva mucho con vos, señora?

I believe I just now saw the glimpse of her. She seems to be an elderly lady.

—Desde ayer sólo, señor.

No, sir; you're mistaken. She's a young lady; and one of the handsomest I ever saw.

—Creo que ahora mismo he visto un vislumbre de ella. Parece dama entrada en años.

Cot so, I beg her pardon! Not but that I should have liked her the better, were she to stay longer, if she had been elderly. I have a strange taste, madam, you'll say, but I really, for my wife's sake, love every elderly woman. Indeed I ever thought age was to be reverenced, which made me (taking the fortune into the scale too, that I own) make my addresses to my present dear.

—No, señor, os equivocáis. Es joven dama, y de las más hermosas que jamás vi.

Very good of you, sir, to respect age: we all hope to live to be old.

—¡Cáspita! ¡Pido su perdón! No es que no me hubiera gustado más, si hubiera de quedarse más tiempo, siendo entrada en años. Tengo un gusto extraño, señora, diréis; mas realmente, por causa de mi esposa, amo a toda mujer entrada en años. En verdad siempre pensé que la edad ha de reverenciarse, lo cual me hizo (metiendo también la fortuna en la balanza, eso lo reconozco) dirigir mis galanteos a mi presente querida.

Right, madam. But you say the lady is beautiful. Now you must know, that though I choose to converse with the elderly, yet I love to see a beautiful young woman, just as I love to see fine flowers in a garden. There's no casting an eye upon her, is there, without her notice? For in this dress, and thus muffled up about my jaws, I should not care to be seen, any more than she, let her love privacy as much as she will.

—Muy bueno de vuestra parte, señor, respetar la edad: todos esperamos vivir para ser viejos.

I will go ask, if I may show a gentleman the apartment, sir; and, as you are a married gentleman, and not over-young, she'll perhaps make the less scruple.

—Bien dicho, señora. Mas decís que la dama es hermosa. Ahora habéis de saber que, aunque escojo conversar con las entradas en años, amo, con todo, ver a una hermosa joven mujer, justo como amo ver finas flores en un jardín. ¿No hay modo de echarle un ojo sin que ella lo advierta? Pues con este vestido, y así arrebujado en cuanto a las quijadas, no me gustaría ser visto, como tampoco a ella, por mucho que ame lo privado.

Then, like me, she loves elderly folks best, perhaps. But it may be she has suffered by young ones?

—Iré a preguntar si puedo mostrar el aposento a un caballero, señor; y, siendo vos caballero casado y no demasiado joven, quizá haga menos escrúpulo.

I fancy she has, sir, or is afraid she shall. She desired to be very private, and if by description inquired after, to be denied.

—Entonces, como yo, ama más a las gentes entradas en años, quizá. Mas puede ser que haya padecido por las jóvenes.

Thou art true woman, goody Moore, thought I!

—Me figuro que ha padecido, señor, o teme padecer. Deseó estar muy privada, y, si se preguntaba por ella por descripción, ser negada.

Good lack!---Good lack!---What may be her story then, I pray?

«Eres verdadera mujer, tía Moore», pensé.

She is pretty reserved in her story; but, to tell you my thoughts, I believe love is in the case: she is always in tears, and does not much care for company.

—¡Válgame! ¡Válgame! ¿Cuál puede ser entonces su historia, os ruego?

Nay, madam, it becomes not me to dive into ladies' secrets; I want not to pry into other people's affairs. But, pray, how does she employ herself?---Yet she came but yesterday; so you can't tell.

—Es bastante reservada en su historia; mas, a deciros mis pensamientos, creo que hay amor en el caso: está siempre en lágrimas, y no se cuida mucho de compañía.

Writing continually, sir.

—A fe, señora, que no me toca a mí bucear en los secretos de las damas; no quiero fisgar en los asuntos ajenos. Mas, os ruego: ¿cómo se emplea? Con todo, no llegó sino ayer; conque no podéis decirlo.

These women, Jack, when you ask them questions by way of information, don't care to be ignorant of anything.

—Escribiendo de continuo, señor.

Nay, excuse me, madam, I am very far from being an inquisitive man. But if her case be difficult, and not merely love, as she is a friend of yours, I would give her my advice.

Estas mujeres, Jack, cuando les haces preguntas por vía de informarte, no gustan de ser ignorantes de nada.

Then you are a lawyer, sir---

—Nay, excusadme, señora, estoy muy lejos de ser hombre inquisitivo. Mas, si su caso es difícil, y no meramente de amor, como es amiga vuestra, le daría mi consejo.

Why, indeed, madam, I was sometime at the Bar; but I have long left practice; yet am much consulted by my friends in difficult points. In a pauper case I frequently give money; but never take any from the richest.

—Entonces sois abogado, señor.

You are a very good gentleman, then, sir.

—Pues, en efecto, señora, estuve algún tiempo en el foro; mas largo tiempo ha que dejé el ejercicio; y, con todo, mis amigos me consultan mucho en puntos difíciles. En causa de pobres frecuentemente doy dinero; mas nunca tomo ninguno de los más ricos.

Ay, madam, we cannot live always here; and we ought to do what good we can---But I hate to appear officious. If the lady stays any time, and thinks fit, upon better acquaintance, to let me in to her case, it may be a happy day for her if I find it a just one; for, you must know, that when I was at the Bar, I never was such a sad fellow as to undertake, for the sake of a paltry fee, to make white black and black white; for what would that have been, but to endeavour to establish iniquity by quirks while I robbed the innocent?

—Sois entonces muy buen caballero, señor.

You are an excellent gentleman, sir: I wish (and then she sighed) I had had the happiness to know there was such a lawyer in the world; and to have been acquainted with him.

—Ay, señora, no podemos vivir aquí siempre; y debemos hacer el bien que podamos. Mas odio parecer oficioso. Si la dama se queda algún tiempo, y tiene a bien, sobre mejor conocimiento, ponerme al tanto de su caso, puede ser feliz día para ella si lo hallo justo; pues habéis de saber que, cuando estaba yo en el foro, nunca fui tan triste sujeto que emprendiera, por un mísero honorario, hacer blanco lo negro y negro lo blanco; pues ¿qué habría sido eso sino esforzarme en establecer la iniquidad con argucias mientras robaba al inocente?

Come, come, Mrs Moore, I think your name is, it may not be too late---when you and I are better acquainted, I may help you perhaps.---But mention nothing of this to the lady; for, as I said, I hate to appear officious.

—Sois excelente caballero, señor. Quisiera (y entonces suspiró) haber tenido la felicidad de saber que había tal abogado en el mundo, y de haberle tratado.

This prohibition, I knew, if goody Moore answered the specimen she had given of her womanhood, would make her take the first opportunity to tell, were it to be necessary to my purpose that she should.

—Vamos, vamos, señora Moore, creo que ese es vuestro nombre: puede no ser demasiado tarde. Cuando vos y yo nos conozcamos mejor, quizá pueda ayudaros a vos. Mas no mencionéis nada de esto a la dama; pues, como he dicho, odio parecer oficioso.

I appeared, upon the whole, so indifferent about seeing the room, or the lady, that the good woman was the more eager I should see both. And the rather, as I, to stimulate her, declared that there was more required in my eye to merit the character of a handsome woman, than most people thought necessary; and that I had never seen six truly lovely ladies in my life.

Esta prohibición, bien lo sabía, si la tía Moore respondía a la muestra que había dado de su condición de mujer, la haría tomar la primera oportunidad de decirlo, si fuera necesario a mi propósito que lo dijera.

To be brief, she went in; and after a little while came out again. The lady, sir, is retired to her closet, so you may go in and look at the room.

Parecí, en conjunto, tan indiferente sobre ver el aposento, o la dama, que la buena mujer estuvo tanto más ávida de que viera ambos. Y tanto más cuanto que yo, por estimularla, declaré que se requería más a mis ojos para merecer el carácter de mujer hermosa de lo que la mayoría de las gentes tienen por necesario, y que nunca en mi vida había visto seis damas verdaderamente encantadoras.

Then how my heart began again to play its pug's tricks!

Por ser breve: entró; y, al cabo de un rato, salió de nuevo.

I hobbled in, and stumped about, and liked it very much; and was sure my wife would. I begged excuse for sitting down, and asked who was the minister of the place? If he were a good preacher? Who preached at the chapel? And if he were a good preacher, and good liver too, madam---I must inquire after that: for I love, I must needs say, that the clergy should practise what they preach.

—La dama, señor, se ha retirado a su gabinete; conque podéis entrar y mirar el aposento.

Very right, sir; but that is not so often the case as were to be wished.

¡Cómo empezó entonces mi corazón a hacer de nuevo sus tretas de monillo!

More's the pity, madam. But I have a great veneration for the clergy in general. It is more a satire upon human nature than upon the cloth, if we suppose those who have the best opportunities to be good, less perfect than other people. For my part, I don't love professional any more than national reflections---But I keep the lady in her closet. My gout makes me rude.

Entré renqueando, y anduve dando trompicones, y me gustó mucho, y estaba seguro de que a mi esposa le gustaría. Rogué que se me excusara por sentarme, y pregunté quién era el ministro del lugar; si era buen predicador; quién predicaba en la capilla; y si él era buen predicador y buen vividor también, señora.

Then up from my seat stumped I---What do you call these window-curtains, madam?

—He de indagar eso, pues amo, he de decirlo por fuerza, que el clero practique lo que predica.

Stuff-damask, Sir.

—Muy bien, señor; mas no es eso tan a menudo el caso como fuera de desear.

It looks mighty well, truly. I like it better than silk. It is warmer to be sure, and much fitter for lodgings in the country; especially for people in years. The bed is in a pretty taste.

—Tanto mayor lástima, señora. Mas tengo gran veneración por el clero en general. Es más sátira contra la naturaleza humana que contra el hábito, si suponemos que quienes tienen las mejores oportunidades de ser buenos son menos perfectos que las demás gentes. Por mi parte, no amo las reflexiones profesionales más que las nacionales. Mas tengo a la dama en su gabinete. Mi gota me hace rudo.

It is neat and clean, sir: that's all we pretend to.

Entonces, levantándome de mi asiento a trompicones:

Ay, mighty well---very well---a silk camlet, I think---very well, truly!---I am sure my wife will like it. But we would not turn the lady out of her lodging for the world. The other two apartments will do for us at the present.

—¿Cómo llamáis a estas cortinas de ventana, señora?

Then stumping towards the closet, over the door of which hung a picture---What picture is that?---Oh! I see: A St Cecilia!

—Damasco de lana, señor.

A common print, sir---

—Muy bien parece, en verdad. Me gusta más que la seda. Es más cálido, de seguro, y mucho más apto para alojamientos en el campo, especialmente para gentes entradas en años. El lecho es de lindo gusto.

Pretty well, pretty well! It is after an Italian master---I would not for the world turn the lady out of her apartment. We can make shift with the other two, repeated I, louder still: but yet mumblingly hoarse; for I had as great regard to uniformity in accent, as to my words.

—Es pulcro y limpio, señor: a eso sólo pretendemos.

Oh Belford! to be so near my angel, think what a painful constraint I was under!---

—Ay, muy bien; muy bien. Camelote de seda, creo. ¡Muy bien, en verdad! Estoy seguro de que a mi esposa le gustará. Mas no echaríamos a la dama de su alojamiento por nada del mundo. Los otros dos aposentos nos servirán al presente.

I was resolved to fetch her out, if possible: and pretending to be going---You can't agree as to any time, Mrs Moore, when we can have this third room, can you?---Not that (whispered I, loud enough to be heard in the next room); not that I would incommode the lady: but I would tell my wife whenabouts ---and women, you know, Mrs Moore, love to have everything before them of this nature.

Entonces, avanzando a trompicones hacia el gabinete, sobre cuya puerta colgaba un cuadro:

Mrs Moore, says my charmer (and never did her voice sound so harmonious to me. Oh how my heart bounded again! It even talked to me, in a manner; for I thought I heard, as well as felt, its unruly flutters; and every vein about me seemed a pulse): Mrs Moore, you may acquaint the gentleman that I shall stay here only for two or three days, at most, till I receive an answer to a letter I have written into the country; and rather than be your hindrance, I will take up with any apartment a pair of stairs higher.

—¿Qué cuadro es ese? ¡Oh, ya veo: una santa Cecilia!

Not for the world! Not for the world, young lady, cried I!---My wife, well as I love her, should lie in a garret, rather than put such a considerate lady as you seem to be, to the least inconveniency.

—Un grabado común, señor.

She opened not the door yet; and I said, But since you have so much goodness, madam, if I could but just look into the closet, as I stand, I could tell my wife whether it is large enough to hold a cabinet she much values, and will have with her wherever she goes.

—¡Bastante bien, bastante bien! Es según un maestro italiano. No echaría a la dama de su aposento por nada del mundo. Podemos arreglárnoslas con los otros dos —repetí, aún más alto, mas con todo mascullantemente ronco; pues tenía tanto miramiento a la uniformidad en el acento como a mis palabras.

Then my charmer opened the door, and blazed upon me, as it were in a flood of light, like what one might imagine would strike a man who, born blind, had by some propitious power been blessed with his sight, all at once, in a meridian sun.

¡Oh, Belford! Estar tan cerca de mi ángel: ¡piensa bajo qué penosa constricción me hallaba!

Upon my soul, I never was so strangely affected before. I had much ado to forbear discovering myself that instant: but, hesitatingly, and in great disorder, I said, looking into the closet, and around it, There is room, I see, for my wife's cabinet; and it has many jewels in it of high price; but, upon my soul (for I could not forbear swearing, like a puppy:---habit is a cursed thing, Jack)---nothing so valuable as the lady I see, can be brought into it!---

Estaba resuelto a hacerla salir, si era posible; y, pretendiendo irme:

She started, and looked at me with terror. The truth of the compliment, as far as I know, had taken dissimulation from my accent.

—¿No podéis convenir en tiempo alguno, señora Moore, en que podamos tener este tercer aposento? No es que —susurré, bastante alto para que se oyera en el cuarto contiguo—, no es que yo quisiera incomodar a la dama; mas querría decir a mi esposa hacia cuándo; y las mujeres, ya lo sabéis, señora Moore, aman tenerlo todo por delante en esta materia.

I saw it was impossible to conceal myself longer from her, any more than (from the violent impulses of my passion) to forbear manifesting myself. I unbuttoned therefore my cape, I pulled off my flapped, slouched hat; I threw open my greatcoat and, like the devil in Milton (an odd comparison though!),

—Señora Moore —dice mi encantadora (y nunca su voz me sonó tan armoniosa; ¡oh, cómo saltó de nuevo mi corazón! Hasta me hablaba, en cierto modo, pues me pareció oír, así como sentir, sus indóciles aleteos; y cada vena mía parecía un pulso)—: señora Moore, podéis hacer saber al caballero que sólo estaré aquí dos o tres días a lo sumo, hasta recibir respuesta a una carta que he escrito al campo; y, antes que ser estorbo vuestro, me contentaré con cualquier aposento un tramo de escalera más arriba.

I started up in my own form divine,

—¡Por nada del mundo! ¡Por nada del mundo, joven dama! —exclamé—. Mi esposa, por bien que la ame, dormiría en una buhardilla antes que poner a dama tan considerada como parecéis ser en la menor inconveniencia.

Touched by the beam of her celestial eye,

Aún no abría ella la puerta; y dije:

More potent than Ithuriel's spear!---

—Mas, ya que tenéis tanta bondad, señora, si pudiera sólo mirar al gabinete desde donde estoy, podría decir a mi esposa si es bastante grande para contener un bufete que valora mucho, y que llevará consigo dondequiera que vaya.

Now, Belford, for a similitude---now for a likeness to illustrate the surprising scene, and the effect it had upon my charmer and the gentlewoman!---But nothing was like it, or equal to it. The plain fact can only describe it, and set it off. Thus then take it.

Entonces mi encantadora abrió la puerta, y resplandeció ante mí, como quien dice, en un raudal de luz, como lo que uno imaginaría que heriría a un hombre que, nacido ciego, hubiera sido bendecido por algún propicio poder con su vista, todo de una vez, bajo un sol de mediodía.

She no sooner saw who it was, than she gave three violent screams; and, before I could catch her in my arms (as I was about to do the moment I discovered myself), down she sunk at my feet in a fit; which made me curse my indiscretion for so suddenly, and with so much emotion, revealing myself.

Por mi alma que nunca antes estuve tan extrañamente afectado. Bien me costó abstenerme de descubrirme en aquel instante; mas, vacilando y en gran desorden, dije, mirando el gabinete y en torno a él:

The gentlewoman, seeing so strange an alteration in my person, and features, and voice, and dress, cried out, Murder, help! Murder, help! by turns, for half a dozen times running. This alarmed the house, and up ran two servant-maids, and my servant after them. I cried out for water and hartshorn, and everyone flew a different way, one of the maids as fast down as she came up; while the gentlewoman ran out of one room into another, and by turns up and down the apartment we were in, without meaning or end, wringing her foolish hands, and not knowing what she did.

—Hay sitio, ya lo veo, para el bufete de mi esposa; y tiene en él muchas joyas de alto precio; mas, por mi alma (pues no pude abstenerme de jurar, como un cachorro: el hábito es cosa maldita, Jack), ¡nada tan valioso como la dama que veo puede meterse en él!

Up then came running a gentleman and his sister, fetched and brought in by the maid who had run down; and who having let in a cursed crabbed old wretch, hobbling with his gout and mumbling with his hoarse broken-toothed voice, was metamorphosed all at once into a lively gay young fellow, with a clear accent, and all his teeth; and she would have it that I was neither more nor less than the devil, and could not keep her eye from my foot; expecting, no doubt, every minute to see it discover itself to be cloven.

Se sobresaltó y me miró con terror. La verdad del cumplido, hasta donde alcanzo, había quitado la disimulación a mi acento.

For my part, I was so intent upon restoring my angel that I regarded nobody else. And at last, she slowly recovering motion, with bitter sighs and sobs (only the whites of her eyes however appearing for some moments), I called upon her in the tenderest accent, as I kneeled by her, my arm supporting her head; My angel! My charmer! My Clarissa! look upon me, my dearest life!---I am not angry with you!---I will forgive you, my best beloved!---

Vi que era imposible ocultarme más tiempo de ella, como tampoco (por los violentos impulsos de mi pasión) abstenerme de manifestarme. Me desabotoné, pues, la esclavina; me quité el calado sombrero de galón; abrí de par en par mi gabán; y, como el diablo en Milton (¡rara comparación, no obstante!),

The gentleman and his sister knew not what to make of all this: and the less, when my fair one, recovering her sight, snatched another look at me; and then again groaned, and fainted away.

me alcé de un salto en mi propia forma divina,
tocado por el rayo de su celestial ojo,
¡más potente que la lanza de Ituriel!

I threw up the closet-sash for air, and then left her to the care of the young gentlewoman, the same notable Miss Rawlins, whom I had heard of at the Flask; and to that of Mrs Moore; who by this time had recovered herself; and then retiring to one corner of the room, I made my servant pull off my gouty stockings, brush my hat, and loop it up into the usual smart cock.

Ahora, Belford, un símil; ahora una semejanza que ilustre la sorprendente escena, y el efecto que tuvo sobre mi encantadora y sobre la señora. Mas nada fue como ella, ni igual a ella. El llano hecho sólo puede describirla y realzarla. Tómalo, pues, así.

I then stepped to the closet to Mr Rawlins, whom, in the general confusion, I had not much minded before.---Sir, said I, you have an uncommon scene before you. The lady is my wife, and no gentleman's presence is necessary here but my own.

No bien vio quién era, dio tres violentos chillidos; y, antes de que pudiera cogerla en mis brazos (como estaba a punto de hacer en el momento en que me descubrí), se hundió a mis pies en un desmayo; lo cual me hizo maldecir mi indiscreción por revelarme tan súbitamente y con tanta emoción.

I beg pardon, sir: If the lady is your wife, I have no business here. But, sir, by her concern at seeing you---

La señora, viendo alteración tan extraña en mi persona, y facciones, y voz, y vestido, gritó: «¡Asesinato! ¡Auxilio! ¡Asesinato! ¡Auxilio!», por turnos, media docena de veces seguidas. Esto alarmó a la casa, y subieron corriendo dos criadas, y mi criado tras ellas. Yo gritaba pidiendo agua y espíritu de cuerno de ciervo, y cada cual voló en dirección distinta; una de las criadas, tan aprisa abajo como había subido; mientras la señora corría de un aposento a otro, y por turnos arriba y abajo del cuarto en que estábamos, sin sentido ni fin, retorciéndose las necias manos y sin saber lo que hacía.

Pray, sir, none of your if's, and but's, I beseech you: nor your concern about the lady's concern. You are a very qualified judge in this cause; and I beg of you, sir, to oblige me with your absence. The ladies only are proper to be present on this occasion, added I; and I think myself obliged to them for their care and kind assistance.

Subieron entonces corriendo un caballero y su hermana, buscados y traídos por la criada que había bajado corriendo; la cual, habiendo hecho entrar a un maldito y cascarrabias viejo miserable, renqueando de gota y mascullando con su ronca voz desdentada, le vio metamorfoseado de una vez en un vivo y alegre joven sujeto, de claro acento y con todos sus dientes; y sostenía que yo no era ni más ni menos que el diablo, y no podía apartar el ojo de mi pie, esperando sin duda a cada minuto verlo descubrirse hendido.

'Tis well he made not another word: for I found my choler begin to rise. I could not bear that the finest neck, and arms, and foot, in the world, should be exposed to the eyes of any man living but mine.

Por mi parte, estaba yo tan intento en restaurar a mi ángel que no reparé en nadie más. Y al fin, recobrando ella lentamente el movimiento, con amargos suspiros y sollozos (aunque sólo lo blanco de sus ojos aparecía por unos momentos), la llamé en el más tierno acento, arrodillado junto a ella, sosteniendo mi brazo su cabeza:

I withdrew once more from the closet, finding her beginning to recover, lest the sight of me too soon should throw her back again.

—¡Ángel mío! ¡Encantadora mía! ¡Mi Clarissa! ¡Miradme, mi queridísima vida! ¡No estoy airado con vos! ¡Os perdonaré, mi mejor amada!

The first words she said, looking round her with great emotion, were, Oh hide me! hide me! Is he gone!---Oh hide me! Is he gone!

El caballero y su hermana no sabían qué hacer de todo esto; y menos aún cuando mi bella, recobrando la vista, me echó otra mirada, y entonces gimió de nuevo y se desmayó.

Sir, said Miss Rawlins, coming to me with an air somewhat peremptory and assured, this is some surprising case. The lady cannot bear the sight of you. What you have done is best known to yourself. But another such fit will probably be her last. It would be but kind, therefore, for you to retire.

Abrí de golpe la vidriera del gabinete para dar aire, y luego la dejé al cuidado de la joven señora —la misma notable señorita Rawlins de quien había oído hablar en el Flask— y de la señora Moore, que para entonces se había recobrado; y, retirándome después a un rincón del cuarto, hice a mi criado quitarme las gotosas medias, cepillarme el sombrero y recogerlo en su airoso doblez de costumbre.

It behoved me to have so notable a person of my party; and the rather, as I had disobliged her impertinent brother.

Pasé entonces al gabinete, al señor Rawlins, en quien, en la general confusión, no había reparado mucho antes.

The dear creature, said I, may well be concerned to see me. If you, madam, had a husband who loved you, as I love her, you would not, I am confident, fly from him and expose yourself to hazards, as she does whenever she has not all her way---and yet with a mind not capable of intentional evil---But, mother-spoilt! This is her fault, and all her fault: and the more inexcusable it is, as I am the man of her choice, and have reason to think she loves me above all the men in the world.

—Señor —dije—, tenéis ante vos una escena poco común. La dama es mi esposa, y ninguna presencia de caballero es aquí necesaria sino la mía.

Here, Jack, was a story to support to the lady; face to face too!^**^

—Pido perdón, señor. Si la dama es vuestra esposa, nada tengo que hacer aquí. Mas, señor, por su preocupación al veros...

You speak like a gentleman; you look like a gentleman, said Miss Rawlins---But, sir, this is a strange case; the lady seems to dread the sight of you.

—Os ruego, señor, ninguno de vuestros síes ni de vuestros peros, os lo suplico; ni vuestra preocupación por la preocupación de la dama. Sois juez muy calificado en esta causa; y os ruego, señor, que me obliguéis con vuestra ausencia. Sólo las damas son propias para estar presentes en esta ocasión —añadí—; y me tengo por obligado a ellas por su cuidado y su bondadosa asistencia.

No wonder, madam; taking her a little on one side, nearer to Mrs Moore. I have three times already forgiven the dear creature---But this jealousy ---there is a spice of that in it---and of frenzy too (whispered I, that it might have the face of a secret, and of consequence the more engage their attention)---but our story is too long---

Bien hizo en no decir otra palabra, pues hallé que mi cólera empezaba a subir. No podía soportar que el más fino cuello, y brazos, y pie del mundo se expusieran a los ojos de hombre alguno viviente sino a los míos.

I then made a motion to go to the lady. But they desired that I would walk into the next room; and they would endeavour to prevail upon her to lie down.

Me retiré una vez más del gabinete, hallando que ella empezaba a recobrarse, no fuera que verme demasiado pronto la hiciera recaer.

I begged that they would not suffer her to talk; for that she was accustomed to fits and would, when in this way, talk of anything that came uppermost; and the more she was suffered to run on, the worse she was; and if not kept quiet would fall into ravings; which might possibly hold her a week.

Las primeras palabras que dijo, mirando en torno suyo con gran emoción, fueron:

They promised to keep her quiet; and I withdrew into the next room; ordering everyone down but Mrs Moore and Miss Rawlins.

—¡Oh, escondedme! ¡Escondedme! ¿Se ha ido? ¡Oh, escondedme! ¿Se ha ido?

She was full of exclamations. Unhappy creature! miserable! ruined! and undone! she called herself; wrung her hands, and begged they would assist her to escape from the terrible evils she should otherwise be made to suffer.

—Señor —dijo la señorita Rawlins, acercándose a mí con aire algo perentorio y seguro—: este es un caso sorprendente. La dama no puede soportar vuestra vista. Lo que hayáis hecho, vos lo sabéis mejor. Mas otro desmayo semejante será probablemente el último. Sería, por tanto, sólo bondadoso que os retiraseis.

They preached patience and quietness to her; and would have had her to lie down; but she refused; sinking, however, into an easy chair; for she trembled so, she could not stand.

Me incumbía tener de mi partido a persona tan notable, y tanto más cuanto que había desobligado a su impertinente hermano.

By this time, I hoped that she was enough recovered to bear a presence, that it behoved me to make her bear; and fearing she would throw out something in her exclamations that would still more disconcert me, I went into the room again.

—La querida criatura —dije— bien puede estar preocupada de verme. Si vos, señora, tuvierais un marido que os amara como yo la amo a ella, no huiríais de él, estoy seguro, ni os expondríais a azares, como ella hace siempre que no puede tenerlo todo a su modo; y, con todo, con un ánimo no capaz de mal intencionado. ¡Mas malcriada por su madre! Esta es su falta, y toda su falta; y tanto más inexcusable cuanto que soy el hombre de su elección, y tengo razón para pensar que me ama por encima de todos los hombres del mundo.

Oh! there he is! said she, and threw her apron over her face---I cannot see him!---I cannot look upon him!---Begone! begone! touch me not!---

¡Aquí tienes, Jack, una historia que sostener ante la dama, y cara a cara!

For I took her struggling hand, beseeching her to be pacified; and assuring her that I would make all up with her, upon her own terms and wishes.

—Habláis como caballero; parecéis caballero —dijo la señorita Rawlins—. Mas, señor, este es un caso extraño: la dama parece temer vuestra vista.

Base man! said the violent lady, I have no wishes, but never to behold you more! Why must I be thus pursued and haunted? Have you not made me miserable enough already? Despoiled of all succour and help, and of every friend, I am contented to be poor, low, and miserable, so I may be free from your persecutions!---

—No es maravilla, señora —llevándola un poco aparte, más cerca de la señora Moore—. Tres veces he perdonado ya a la querida criatura. Mas estos celos... hay una punta de eso en ello... y también de frenesí —susurré, para que tuviera cara de secreto y por consiguiente empeñara más su atención—; mas nuestra historia es demasiado larga.

Miss Rawlins stared at me (a confident slut this Miss Rawlins, thought I!): so did Mrs Moore---I told you so! whisperingly said I, turning to the women; shaking my head with a face of great concern and pity; and then to my charmer, My dear creature, how you rave!---You will not easily recover from the effects of this violence! Have patience, my love! Be pacified! and we will coolly talk this matter over: for you expose yourself, as well as me. These ladies will certainly think you have fallen among robbers; and that I am the chief of them.

Hice entonces ademán de acercarme a la dama. Mas me rogaron que pasara al cuarto contiguo, y que ellas se esforzarían en prevalecer sobre ella para que se acostara.

So you are! so you are! stamping, her face still covered (she thought of Wednesday night, no doubt); and, sighing as if her heart were breaking, she put her hand to her forehead---I shall be quite distracted!

Les rogué que no le consintieran hablar; pues estaba acostumbrada a los desmayos, y, cuando estaba de aquel modo, hablaba de cuanto le venía a la boca; y cuanto más se le dejara correr, peor estaba; y, si no se la mantenía quieta, caería en desvaríos que podrían posiblemente durarle una semana.

I will not, my dearest love, uncover your face. You shall not look upon me, since I am so odious to you. But this is a violence I never thought you capable of---

Prometieron mantenerla quieta; y me retiré al cuarto contiguo, ordenando a todos bajar salvo a la señora Moore y a la señorita Rawlins.

And I would have pressed her hand, as I held it, with my lips; but she drew it from me with indignation.

Estaba llena de exclamaciones. ¡Desdichada criatura! ¡Miserable! ¡Arruinada y deshecha!, se llamaba a sí misma; se retorcía las manos y les rogaba que la asistieran para escapar de los terribles males que de otro modo se le haría padecer.

Unhand me, sir, said she. I will not be touched by you. Leave me to my fate. What right, what title, have you to persecute me thus?

Ellas le predicaban paciencia y quietud, y querían que se acostara; mas ella rehusó, hundiéndose, no obstante, en un sillón, pues temblaba de tal modo que no podía tenerse en pie.

What right, what title, my dear!---But this is not a time---I have a letter from Captain Tomlinson---Here it is---offering it to her---

Para entonces esperaba yo que estuviera bastante recobrada para soportar una presencia que me incumbía hacerle soportar; y, temiendo que en sus exclamaciones soltara algo que me desconcertara aún más, entré de nuevo en el cuarto.

I will receive nothing from your hands---Tell me not of Captain Tomlinson---Tell me not of anybody---You have no right to invade me thus---Once more, leave me to my fate---Have you not made me miserable enough?---

—¡Oh, ahí está! —dijo, y se echó el delantal sobre el rostro—. ¡No puedo verle! ¡No puedo mirarle! ¡Idos! ¡Idos! ¡No me toquéis!

I touched a delicate string, on purpose to set her in such a passion before the women as might confirm the intimation I had given of a frenzical disorder.

Pues yo había tomado su forcejeante mano, suplicándole que se apaciguara y asegurándole que lo compondría todo con ella, en sus propios términos y deseos.

What a turn is here!---Lately so happy!---Nothing wanting but a reconciliation between you and your friends!---that reconciliation in such a happy train!---shall so slight, so accidental an occasion be suffered to overturn all our happiness?

—¡Vil hombre! —dijo la violenta dama—: no tengo deseos, sino no volver a contemplaros nunca. ¿Por qué he de ser así perseguida y acosada? ¿No me habéis hecho ya bastante desdichada? Despojada de todo socorro y auxilio, y de todo amigo, me contento con ser pobre, baja y miserable, ¡con tal de verme libre de vuestras persecuciones!

She started up with a trembling impatience, her apron falling from her indignant face---Now, said she, that thou darest to call the occasion slight and accidental, and that I am happily out of thy vile hands, and out of a house I have reason to believe as vile, traitor and wretch that thou art, I will venture to cast an eye upon thee---and Oh that it were in my power, in mercy to my sex, to look thee first into shame and remorse, and then into death!

La señorita Rawlins me miró fijamente (¡descarada bribona, esta señorita Rawlins, pensé!); y también la señora Moore.

This violent tragedy speech, and the high manner in which she uttered it, had its desired effect. I looked upon the women, and upon her, by turns, with a pitying eye; and they shook their wise heads, and besought me to retire, and her to lie down to compose herself.

—¡Ya os lo dije! —susurré, volviéndome a las mujeres, meneando la cabeza con rostro de gran preocupación y piedad. Y luego a mi encantadora—: ¡Mi querida criatura, cómo desvariáis! ¡No os recobraréis fácilmente de los efectos de esta violencia! ¡Tened paciencia, mi amor! ¡Apaciguaos! Y hablaremos fríamente de este asunto; pues os exponéis a vos misma, así como a mí. Estas damas pensarán ciertamente que habéis caído entre ladrones, y que yo soy el principal de ellos.

This hurricane, like other hurricanes, was presently allayed by a shower. She threw herself once more into her armed chair---and begged pardon of the women for her passionate excess; but not of me: yet I was in hopes that when compliments were stirring, I should have come in for a share.

—¡Así es! ¡Así es! —dando una patada, aún cubierto el rostro (pensaba en la noche del miércoles, sin duda); y, suspirando como si el corazón se le rompiera, se llevó la mano a la frente—. ¡Quedaré del todo enajenada!

Indeed, ladies, said I (with assurance enough, thou'It say), this violence is not natural to my beloved's temper---misapprehension---

—No os descubriré el rostro, mi queridísima amada. No me miraréis, ya que tan odioso os soy. Mas esta es una violencia de la que nunca os creí capaz.

Misapprehension, wretch!---and want I excuses from thee!

Y habría oprimido su mano con mis labios, teniéndola como la tenía; mas la retiró con indignación.

What a scorn was every lovely feature agitated by!

—Soltadme, señor —dijo—. No seré tocada por vos. Dejadme a mi hado. ¿Qué derecho, qué título tenéis para perseguirme así?

Then turning her face from me, I have not patience, Oh thou guileful betrayer, to look upon thee!---Begone! Begone! With a face so unblushing, how darest thou my presence?

—¿Qué derecho, qué título, mi querida? Mas no es este el tiempo. Tengo carta del capitán Tomlinson. Aquí está —ofreciéndosela.

I thought then that the character of a husband obliged me to be angry.

—No recibiré nada de vuestras manos. No me habléis del capitán Tomlinson. No me habléis de nadie. No tenéis derecho a invadirme así. Una vez más: dejadme a mi hado. ¿No me habéis hecho bastante desdichada?

You may one day, madam, repent this treatment---by my soul you may---You know I have not deserved it of you---you know I have not.

Toqué una delicada cuerda a propósito, para ponerla en tal pasión ante las mujeres que confirmara la insinuación que yo había dado de un desorden frenético.

Do I know you have not?---wretch! Do I know---

—¡Qué giro es este! ¡Tan felices hace poco! ¡Nada faltando sino una reconciliación entre vos y vuestros parientes! ¡Aquella reconciliación en tan feliz camino! ¿Ha de consentirse que ocasión tan leve, tan accidental, eche por tierra toda nuestra felicidad?

You do, madam!---and never did man of my figure and consideration (I thought it was proper to throw that in) meet with such treatment. (She lifted up her hands: indignation kept her silent)---But all is of a piece with the charge you bring against me of despoiling you of all succour and help, of making you poor and low, and with other unprecedented language. I will only say, before these two gentlewomen, that since it must be so, and since your former esteem for me is turned into so riveted an aversion, I will soon, very soon, make you entirely easy. I will be gone:---I will leave you to your own fate, as you call it; and may that be happy!---Only, that I may not appear to be a spoiler, a robber indeed, let me know whither I shall send your apparel, and everything that belongs to you, and I will send it.

Se levantó de un salto con temblorosa impaciencia, cayéndole el delantal del indignado rostro.

Send it to this place; and assure me that you will never molest me more; never more come near me; and that is all I ask of you.

—Ahora —dijo— que osas llamar leve y accidental a la ocasión, y que estoy felizmente fuera de tus viles manos, y fuera de una casa que tengo razón para creer igual de vil, traidor y miserable que eres, me aventuraré a echarte un ojo encima. ¡Y oh, si estuviera en mi poder, por misericordia hacia mi sexo, mirarte primero hasta la vergüenza y el remordimiento, y luego hasta la muerte!

I will do so, madam, said I, with a dejected air. But did I ever think I should be so indifferent to you?---However, you must permit me to insist on your reading this letter; and on your seeing Captain Tomlinson, and hearing what he has to say from your uncle. He will be here by and by.

Este violento discurso trágico, y la alta manera en que lo profirió, tuvo el efecto deseado. Miré a las mujeres, y a ella, por turnos, con ojo compasivo; y ellas menearon sus sabias cabezas y me suplicaron a mí que me retirara, y a ella que se acostara a componerse.

Don't trifle with me, said she, in an imperious tone---Do as you offer. I will not receive any letter from your hands. If I see Captain Tomlinson, it shall be on his own account; not on yours. You tell me you will send me my apparel: if you would have me believe anything you say, let this be the test of your sincerity---Leave me now, and send my things.

Este huracán, como otros huracanes, se aplacó al punto con un chaparrón. Se arrojó una vez más a su sillón, y pidió perdón a las mujeres por su apasionado exceso; mas no a mí; y, con todo, yo tenía esperanzas de que, cuando se repartieran cumplidos, me tocaría mi parte.

The women stared. They did nothing but stare; and appeared to be more and more at a loss what to make of the matter between us.

—En verdad, señoras —dije (con bastante seguridad, dirás)—, esta violencia no es natural al temple de mi amada. Un malentendido...

I pretended to be going from her in a pet: but when I had got to the door, I turned back; and, as if I had recollected myself, One word more, my dearest creature!---charming even in your anger!---Oh my fond soul! said I, turning half round, and pulling out my handkerchief.

—¡Malentendido, miserable! ¿Y me hacen falta excusas de ti?

I believe, Jack, my eyes did glisten a little---I have no doubt but they did---The women pitied me. Honest souls!---they showed that they had each of them a handkerchief as well as I. So, hast thou not observed (to give a familiar illustration) every man in a company of a dozen or more, obligingly pull out his watch, when some one has asked what's o'clock?

¡Qué desdén agitaba cada encantadora facción!

One word only, madam, repeated I as soon as my voice had recovered its tone---I have represented to Captain Tomlinson in the most favourable light the cause of our present misunderstanding. You know what your uncle insists upon; and which you have acquiesced with. The letter in my hand (and again I offered it to her) will acquaint you with what you have to apprehend from your brother's active malice.

Entonces, apartando de mí el rostro:

She was going to speak in a high accent, putting the letter from her, with an open palm---Nay, hear me out, madam---The captain, you know, has reported our marriage to two different persons. It is come to your brother's ears. My own relations have also heard of it. Letters were brought me from town this morning, from Lady Betty Lawrance and Miss Montague. Here they are (I pulled them out of my pocket, and offered them to her, with that of the captain; but she held back her still open palm, that she might not receive them). Reflect, madam, I beseech you reflect, upon the fatal consequences which this your high resentment may be attended with.

—No tengo paciencia, oh dolosa traidora criatura, ¡para mirarte! ¡Idos! ¡Idos! Con cara tan sin rubor, ¿cómo osas mi presencia?

Ever since I knew you, said she, I have been in a wilderness of doubt and error. I bless God that I am out of your hands. I will transact for myself what relates to myself. I dismiss all your solicitude for me. Am I not my own mistress!---Am I not---

Pensé entonces que el carácter de marido me obligaba a estar airado.

The women stared. (The devil stare ye, thought I, can ye do nothing but stare?) It was high time to stop her here. I raised my voice to drown hers---You used, my dearest creature, to have a tender and apprehensive heart---You never had so much reason for such a one as now.

—Podéis un día, señora, arrepentiros de este trato. Por mi alma que podéis. Sabéis que no lo he merecido de vos; sabéis que no.

Let me judge for myself upon what I shall see, not upon what I shall hear ---Do you think I shall ever---

—¿Sé yo que no lo has merecido? ¡Miserable! ¿Sé yo...?

I dreaded her going on---I must be heard, madam, raising my voice still higher. You must let me read one paragraph or two of this letter to you, if you will not read it yourself---

—Lo sabéis, señora. Y nunca hombre de mi figura y consideración (juzgué propio meter eso) encontró trato semejante. (Alzó las manos: la indignación la tuvo callada.) Mas todo es de una pieza con la acusación que me hacéis de despojaros de todo socorro y auxilio, de haceros pobre y baja, y con otro lenguaje sin precedentes. Sólo diré, ante estas dos señoras, que, ya que ha de ser así, y ya que vuestra anterior estima por mí se ha vuelto en aversión tan remachada, pronto, muy pronto, os dejaré del todo tranquila. Me iré; os dejaré a vuestro propio hado, como lo llamáis; ¡y sea ese feliz! Sólo que, para no parecer un despojador, un verdadero ladrón, hacedme saber adónde he de enviar vuestras ropas, y cuanto os pertenece, y lo enviaré.

Begone from me, man!---Begone from me with thy letters! What pretence hast thou for tormenting me thus---

—Enviadlo a este lugar; y aseguradme que nunca más me molestaréis, que nunca más os acercaréis a mí; y eso es todo cuanto os pido.

Dearest creature, what questions you ask! Questions that you can as well answer yourself---

—Así lo haré, señora —dije, con aire abatido—. ¿Mas pensé yo alguna vez que había de serme tan indiferente? No obstante, habéis de permitirme insistir en que leáis esta carta, y en que veáis al capitán Tomlinson y oigáis lo que tenga que deciros de parte de vuestro tío. Estará aquí dentro de poco.

I can, I will ---And thus I answer them---

—No juguéis conmigo —dijo, en tono imperioso—. Haced lo que ofrecéis. No recibiré carta alguna de vuestras manos. Si veo al capitán Tomlinson, será por cuenta suya, no por la vuestra. Decís que me enviaréis mis ropas: si queréis que crea algo de cuanto decís, sea esta la prueba de vuestra sinceridad. Idos ahora, y enviad mis cosas.

Still louder raised I my voice. She was overborne. Sweet soul! It would be hard, thought I (and yet I was very angry with her), if such a spirit as thine cannot be brought to yield to such a one as mine!

Las mujeres miraban. No hacían sino mirar; y parecían estar cada vez más perdidas sobre qué hacer del asunto entre nosotros.

I lowered my voice on her silence. All gentle, all intreative, my accent: my head bowed; one hand held out; the other on my honest heart---For Heaven's sake, my dearest creature, resolve to see Captain Tomlinson with temper. He would have come along with me: but I was willing to try to soften your mind first, on this fatal misapprehension; and this for the sake of your own wishes: for what is it otherwise to me, whether your friends are, or are not, reconciled to us? Do I want any favour from them? ---For your own mind's sake therefore, frustrate not Captain Tomlin-son's negotiation. That worthy gentleman will be here in the afternoon---Lady Betty will be in town with my cousin Montague in a day or two. They will be your visitors. I beseech you do not carry this misunderstanding so far, as that Lord M. and Lady Betty, and Lady Sarah, may know it. (How considerable this made me look to the women !) Lady Betty will not let you rest till you consent to accompany her to her own seat---and to that lady may you safely entrust your cause.

Fingí apartarme de ella de mal talante; mas, cuando había llegado a la puerta, me volví; y, como si lo hubiera recordado:

Again, upon my pausing a moment, she was going to break out. I liked not the turn of her countenance, nor the tone of her voice---'And thinkest thou, base wretch,' were the words she did utter. I again raised my voice, and drowned hers---Base wretch, madam!---You know that I have not deserved the violent names you have called me. Words so opprobrious from a mind so gentle---but this treatment is from you, madam!---from you, whom I love more than my own soul---By that soul, I swear that I do---(The women looked upon each other. They seemed pleased with my ardour. Women, whether wives, maids, or widows, love ardours. Even Miss Howe, thou knowest, speaks up for ardours^**^)---Nevertheless, I must say that you have carried matters too far for the occasion. I see you hate me---

—¡Una palabra más, mi queridísima criatura! ¡Encantadora aun en vuestra cólera! ¡Oh, mi encariñada alma! —dije, volviéndome a medias y sacando el pañuelo.

She was just going to speak---If we are to separate for ever, in a strong and solemn voice, proceeded I, this island shall not long be troubled with me---Meantime, only be pleased to give these letters a perusal, and consider what is to be said to your uncle's friend; and what he is to say to your uncle---Anything will I come into (renounce me if you will), that shall make for your peace, and for the reconciliation your heart was so lately set upon. But I humbly conceive that it is necessary that you should come into better temper with me, were it but to give a favourable appearance to what has passed, and weight to my future application to your friends, in whatever way you shall think proper to make it.

Creo, Jack, que mis ojos sí que relucieron un poco; no tengo duda de que lo hicieron. Las mujeres me compadecieron. ¡Honradas almas! Mostraron que cada una tenía un pañuelo tanto como yo. Así (por dar una familiar ilustración), ¿no has observado que, en compañía de una docena de hombres o más, cada uno saca obligantemente su reloj cuando alguno pregunta qué hora es?

I then put the letters into her lap, and retired into the next apartment with a low bow, and a very solemn air.

—Una sola palabra, señora —repetí en cuanto mi voz hubo recobrado su tono—. He representado al capitán Tomlinson bajo la luz más favorable la causa de nuestro presente malentendido. Sabéis en qué insiste vuestro tío, y con lo cual habéis aquiescido. La carta que tengo en la mano (y de nuevo se la ofrecí) os hará saber lo que habéis de aprensar de la activa malicia de vuestro hermano.

I was soon followed by the two women. Mrs Moore withdrew to give the fair perverse time to read them: Miss Rawlins for the same reason; and because she was sent for home.

Iba a hablar en alto acento, apartando de sí la carta con la palma abierta.

The widow besought her speedy return. I joined in the same request; and she was ready enough to promise to oblige us.

—Nay, oídme hasta el fin, señora. El capitán, ya lo sabéis, ha comunicado nuestro matrimonio a dos personas distintas. Ha llegado a oídos de vuestro hermano. Mis propios parientes lo han oído también. Se me trajeron cartas de la villa esta mañana, de lady Betty Lawrance y de la señorita Montague. Aquí están (las saqué del bolsillo y se las ofrecí, con la del capitán; mas retiró la aún abierta palma para no recibirlas). Reflexionad, señora, os suplico que reflexionéis sobre las fatales consecuencias de que puede ir acompañado este vuestro alto resentimiento.

I excused myself to Mrs Moore for the disguise I had appeared in at first, and for the story I had invented. I told her that I held myself obliged to satisfy her for the whole floor we were upon; and for an upper room for my servant; and that for a month certain.

—Desde que os conozco —dijo—, he estado en un desierto de dudas y de errores. Bendigo a Dios de estar fuera de vuestras manos. Trataré yo misma lo que a mí misma atañe. Despido toda vuestra solicitud por mí. ¿No soy dueña de mí misma? ¿No soy...?

She made many scruples, and begged she might not be urged on this head till she had consulted Miss Rawlins.

Las mujeres miraban. (¡Que el diablo os mire a vosotras, pensé! ¿No sabéis hacer otra cosa que mirar?) Era muy hora de detenerla ahí. Alcé la voz para ahogar la suya.

I consented; but told her that she had taken my earnest; and I hoped there was no room for dispute.

—Solíais, mi queridísima criatura, tener un corazón tierno y aprensivo. Nunca tuvisteis tanta razón para tal como ahora.

Just then Miss Rawlins returned with an air of eager curiosity; and having been told what had passed between Mrs Moore and me, she gave herself airs of office immediately: which I humoured, plainly perceiving that if I had her with me, I had the other.

—Dejadme juzgar por mí misma sobre lo que vea, no sobre lo que oiga. ¿Creéis que jamás...?

She wished, if there were time for it, and if it were not quite impertinent in her to desire it, that I would give Mrs Moore and her a brief history of an affair which, as she said, bore the face of novelty, mystery, and surprise: for sometimes it looked to her as if we were married; at other times that point appeared doubtful; and yet the lady did not absolutely deny it; but, upon the whole, thought herself highly injured.

Temí que prosiguiera.

I said that ours was a very particular case: that were I to acquaint them with it, some part of it would hardly appear credible. But, however, I would give them, as they seemed to be persons of discretion, a brief account of the whole; and this in so plain and sincere a manner that it should clear up to their satisfaction everything that had passed, or might hereafter pass between us.

—He de ser oído, señora —alzando la voz aún más—. Habéis de dejarme leeros un párrafo o dos de esta carta, si no queréis leerla vos misma.

They sat down by me, and threw every feature of their faces into attention. I was resolved to go as near the truth as possible, lest anything should drop from my spouse to impreach my veracity; and yet keep in view what passed at the Flask.

—¡Idos de mí, hombre! ¡Idos de mí con vuestras cartas! ¿Qué pretexto tenéis para atormentarme así?

It is necessary, although thou knowest my whole story, and a good deal of my views, that thou shouldst be apprised of the substance of what I told them.

—¡Queridísima criatura, qué preguntas hacéis! Preguntas que vos misma podéis responder igual de bien.

'I gave them in as concise a manner as I was able the history of our families, fortunes, alliances, antipathies (her brother's, and mine, particularly). I averred the truth of our private marriage.' The captain's letter, which I will enclose, will give thee my reasons for that: and besides, the women might also, perhaps, have proposed a parson to me by way of compromise. 'I told them the condition my spouse had made me swear to; and which she held me to, in order, I said, to induce me the sooner to be reconciled to her relations.

—Puedo, y lo haré. Y así las respondo.

'I owned that this restraint made me sometimes ready to fly out.' And Mrs Moore was so good as to declare that she did not much wonder at it.

Aún más alto alcé la voz. Quedó vencida. ¡Dulce alma! Sería duro, pensé (y, con todo, estaba yo muy airado con ella), que espíritu como el tuyo no pudiera traerse a ceder a uno como el mío.

Thou art a very good sort of woman, Mrs Moore, thought I.

Bajé la voz al callar ella. Todo gentil, todo implorativo mi acento; inclinada la cabeza; tendida una mano; la otra sobre mi honrado corazón:

As Miss Howe has actually detected our mother; and might possibly find some way still to acquaint her friend with her discoveries; I thought it proper to prepossess them in Mrs Sinclair's favour; and in that of her two nieces.

—Por amor del cielo, mi queridísima criatura, resolveos a ver al capitán Tomlinson con temple. Habría venido conmigo; mas quise probar antes a ablandar vuestro ánimo sobre este fatal malentendido; y esto por causa de vuestros propios deseos. Pues ¿qué me importa a mí, de otro modo, que vuestros parientes estén o no reconciliados con nosotros? ¿Quiero yo favor alguno de ellos? Por causa, pues, de vuestro propio ánimo, no frustréis la gestión del capitán Tomlinson. Aquel digno caballero estará aquí por la tarde. Lady Betty estará en la villa con mi prima Montague dentro de un día o dos. Serán vuestras visitantes. Os suplico que no llevéis este malentendido tan lejos que lord M., y lady Betty, y lady Sarah puedan saberlo. (¡Cuán considerable me hizo esto parecer ante las mujeres!) Lady Betty no os dejará descansar hasta que consintáis en acompañarla a su propia casa; y a aquella dama podéis con seguridad confiar vuestra causa.

I said, 'They were gentlewomen born; had not bad hearts; that indeed my spouse did not love them; they having once jointly taken the liberty to blame her for her over-niceness with regard to me. People, I said, even good people, who knew themselves to be guilty of a fault they had no inclination to mend, were too often least patient when told of it; as they could less bear than others to be thought indifferently of.'

De nuevo, al detenerme yo un momento, iba ella a prorrumpir. No me gustó el giro de su semblante, ni el tono de su voz.

Too often the case, they owned.

—«¿Y crees, vil miserable...?» —fueron las palabras que sí profirió.

'Mrs Sinclair's house was a very handsome house, and fit to receive the first quality. (True enough, Jack!) Mrs Sinclair was a woman very easy in her circumstances: a widow-gentlewoman---as you, Mrs Moore, are. Lets lodgings---as you, Mrs Moore, do. Once had better prospects---as you, Mrs Moore, may have had: the relict of Colonel Sinclair: you, Mrs Moore, might know Colonel Sinclair---he had lodgings at Hampstead.'

De nuevo alcé la voz y ahogué la suya.

She had heard of the name.

—¡Vil miserable, señora! Sabéis que no he merecido los violentos nombres que me habéis llamado. Palabras tan oprobiosas de un ánimo tan gentil... ¡Mas este trato viene de vos, señora! ¡De vos, a quien amo más que a mi propia alma! ¡Por aquella alma juro que lo hago! (Las mujeres se miraron una a otra. Parecieron complacidas con mi ardor. Las mujeres, ya sean esposas, doncellas o viudas, aman los ardores. Hasta la señorita Howe, bien lo sabes, habla en favor de los ardores.) No obstante, he de decir que habéis llevado las cosas demasiado lejos para la ocasión. Ya veo que me odiáis.

'Oh, he was related to the best families in Scotland: and his widow is not to be reflected upon because she lets lodgings, you know Mrs Moore;---you know, Miss Rawlins.'

Iba justo a hablar.

Very true, and, very true: and they must needs say, it did not look quite so pretty in such a lady as my spouse, to be so censorious.

—Si hemos de separarnos para siempre —proseguí, con voz fuerte y solemne—, esta isla no se verá largo tiempo molestada conmigo. Entre tanto, tened sólo a bien dar a estas cartas una lectura, y considerar qué ha de decirse al amigo de vuestro tío, y qué ha de decir él a vuestro tío. En cualquier cosa entraré (renunciadme si queréis) que haga por vuestra paz, y por la reconciliación en que tan recientemente teníais puesto el corazón. Mas humildemente concibo que es necesario que vengáis a mejor temple conmigo, aunque no fuera sino para dar apariencia favorable a lo pasado, y peso a mi futura gestión ante vuestros parientes, del modo que juzguéis propio hacerla.

A foundation here, thought I, to procure these women's help to get back the fugitive, or their connivance at least at my doing so; as well as for anticipating any future information from Miss Howe.

Puse entonces las cartas en su regazo, y me retiré al aposento contiguo con una honda reverencia y aire muy solemne.

I gave them a character of that virago: and intimated, 'that for a head to contrive mischief, and a heart to execute it, she had hardly her equal in her sex.'

Pronto me siguieron las dos mujeres. La señora Moore se retiró para dar tiempo a la bella perversa de leerlas; la señorita Rawlins, por la misma razón, y porque la llamaban a su casa.

To this Miss Howe it was, Mrs Moore said she supposed, that my spouse was so desirous to dispatch a man and horse, by day-dawn, with a letter she wrote before she went to bed last night; proposing to stay no longer than till she had received an answer to it.

La viuda le suplicó pronta vuelta. Me uní a la misma petición; y ella estuvo bastante pronta a prometer obligarnos.

The very same, said I. I knew she would have immediate recourse to her. I should have been but too happy, could I have prevented such a letter from passing, or so to have managed as to have it given into Mrs Howe's hands instead of her daughter's. Women who had lived some time in the world, knew better than to encourage such skittish pranks in young wives.

Me excusé ante la señora Moore por el disfraz con que había aparecido al principio, y por la historia que había inventado. Le dije que me tenía por obligado a satisfacerle todo el piso en que estábamos, y un cuarto alto para mi criado; y eso por un mes cierto.

Let me just stop to tell thee, while it is in my head, that I have since given Will his cue to find out where the man lives who is gone with the fair fugitive's letter; and, if possible, to see him on his return before he sees her.

Puso muchos escrúpulos, y rogó que no se la urgiera en esta cabeza hasta haber consultado a la señorita Rawlins.

I told the women, 'That I despaired it would ever be better with us while Miss Howe had so strange a predominance over my spouse, and remained herself unmarried; and until the reconciliation with her friends could be effected; or a still happier event---as I should think it, who am the last male of my family; and which my foolish vow, and her rigour, had hitherto'---

Consentí; mas le dije que había tomado mi señal, y esperaba que no hubiera lugar a disputa.

Here I stopped, and looked modest, turning my diamond ring round my finger: while goody Moore looked mighty significant, calling it a very particular case; and the maiden lady fanned away, and primmed and pursed, to show that what I said needed no farther explanation.

Justo entonces volvió la señorita Rawlins con aire de ávida curiosidad; y, habiéndosele contado lo que había pasado entre la señora Moore y yo, se dio al punto aires de oficio; lo cual seguí de buen grado, percibiendo llanamente que, si tenía a ella conmigo, tenía a la otra.

'I told them the occasion of our present difference: avowed the reality of the fire: but owned that I would have made no scruple of breaking the unnatural oath she had bound me in (having a husband's right of my side), when she was so accidentally frighted into my arms: and I blamed myself excessively that I did not; since she thought fit to carry her resentment so high, and had the injustice to suppose the fire to be a contrivance of mine.'

Deseaba, si había tiempo para ello, y si no era en ella del todo impertinente desearlo, que yo diera a la señora Moore y a ella una breve historia de un asunto que, según dijo, tenía cara de novedad, de misterio y de sorpresa; pues a ratos le parecía que estábamos casados, otras veces aquel punto parecía dudoso, y, con todo, la dama no lo negaba absolutamente; mas, en conjunto, se tenía por altamente agraviada.

Nay, for that matter, Mrs Moore said---as we were married, and madam was so odd---every gentleman would not---and there stopped Mrs Moore.

Dije que el nuestro era caso muy particular; que, si hubiera de enterarlas de él, alguna parte apenas parecería creíble. Mas que, no obstante, les daría, ya que parecían personas de discreción, un breve relato del todo; y esto de manera tan llana y sincera que aclarara a su satisfacción cuanto había pasado, o pudiera pasar en adelante, entre nosotros.

'To suppose I should have recourse to such a poor contrivance, said I, when I saw the dear creature every hour ---' Was not this a bold put, Jack?

Se sentaron a mi lado, y echaron cada facción de sus rostros en actitud de atención. Estaba resuelto a ir tan cerca de la verdad como fuera posible, no fuera que se escapara algo de mi esposa que impugnara mi veracidad; y, con todo, a tener a la vista lo que había pasado en el Flask.

A most extraordinary case, truly! the maiden lady: fanning, yet coming in with her Well buts, and her sifting Pray, sir's! ---And her restraining Enough, sir's! ---flying from the question to the question; her seat now and then uneasy, for fear my want of delicacy should hurt her abundant modesty; and yet it was difficult to satisfy her super-abundant curiosity.

Es necesario, aunque conoces toda mi historia y buena parte de mis miras, que quedes apercibido de la sustancia de cuanto les dije.

'My beloved's jealousy; which of itself, to female minds, accounts for a thousand unaccountablenesses; and the imputation of her half-frenzy brought upon her by her father's wicked curse, and by the previous persecutions she had undergone from all her family; were what I dwelt upon in order to provide against what might happen.'

«Les di, del modo más conciso que pude, la historia de nuestras familias, fortunas, alianzas, antipatías (las de su hermano y las mías, particularmente). Aseveré la verdad de nuestro matrimonio privado.» La carta del capitán, que adjuntaré, te dará mis razones para eso; y, además, las mujeres podrían quizá haberme propuesto un párroco por vía de componenda.

In short, 'I owned against myself most of the offences which I did not doubt but she would charge me with in their hearing: and as every cause has a black and white side, I gave the worst parts of our story the gentlest turn. And when I had done, gave them some partial hints of the contents of Captain Tomlinson's letter, which I had left with her: with a caution to be guarded against the inquiries of James Harlowe and of Captain Singleton, or of sailor-looking men.' This thou wilt see from the letter itself was necessary to be done. Here therefore thou mayest read it. And a charming letter to my purpose, if thou givest the least attention to its contents, wilt thou find it to be.

«Les dije la condición que mi esposa me había hecho jurar, y en la cual me tenía, a fin, dije, de inducirme antes a reconciliarme con sus parientes.

\[*Letter 233.1: 'Captain Tomlinson'\] to Robert Lovelace, Esq.*

»Reconocí que esta restricción me ponía a veces pronto a desmandarme.» Y la señora Moore fue tan buena que declaró que no se maravillaba mucho de ello.

Wed. June 7

«Eres mujer de muy buena especie, señora Moore», pensé.

Dear sir,

Como la señorita Howe ha detectado efectivamente a nuestra madre, y podría posiblemente hallar aún modo de enterar a su amiga de sus descubrimientos, juzgué propio predisponerlas en favor de la señora Sinclair y de sus dos sobrinas.

ALTHOUGH I am obliged to be in town tomorrow, or next day at farthest, yet I would not dispense with writing to you by one of my servants (whom I send up before me upon a particular occasion), in order to advertise you that it is probable you will hear from some of your own relations on your (supposed') nuptials. One of the persons (Mr Lilburne by name) to whom I hinted my belief of your marriage, happens to be acquainted with Mr Spurrier, Lady Betty Lawrance's steward; and (not being under any restriction) mentioned it to Mr Spurrier, and he to Lady Betty, as a thing certain: and this (though I have not the honour to be personally known to her ladyship) brought on an inquiry from her ladyship to me by her gentleman; who coming to me in company with Mr Lilburne, I had no way but to confirm the report. And I understand that Lady Betty takes it amiss, that she was not acquainted with so desirable a piece of news from yourself.

Dije «que eran nacidas señoras; que no tenían mal corazón; que en efecto mi esposa no las amaba, habiéndose ellas tomado una vez juntamente la libertad de censurarla por su exceso de melindre conmigo. Las gentes, dije, aun las gentes buenas, que se saben culpables de una falta que no tienen inclinación a enmendar, son demasiado a menudo las menos pacientes cuando se les dice de ella; ya que soportan menos que otras que se piense indiferentemente de ellas».

Her ladyship, it seems, has business that calls her to town; (and you will possibly choose to put her right. If you do, it will, I presume, be in confidence; that nothing may perspire from your own family to contradict what I have given out.)

Demasiado a menudo el caso, reconocieron.

(I have ever been of opinion, that truth ought to be strictly adhered to on all occasions: and am concerned that I have departed (though with so good a view), from my old maxim. But my dear friend Mr John Harlowe would have it so. Yet I never knew a departure of this kind a single departure. But, to make the best of it now, allow me, sir, once more to beg the lady as soon as possible to authenticate the report given out.) When you both join in the acknowledgement \[of your marriage\], it will be impertinent in anyone to be inquisitive as to the day or week: (and, if as privately celebrated as you intend, while the gentlewomen with whom you lodge are properly instructed as you say they are, and who actually believe you are married long ago, who shall be able to give a contradiction to my report?)

«La casa de la señora Sinclair era casa muy hermosa, y apta para recibir a la primera calidad. (¡Bastante cierto, Jack!) La señora Sinclair era mujer desahogada en sus circunstancias: señora viuda, como vos, señora Moore. Alquila alojamientos, como vos, señora Moore, hacéis. Tuvo un tiempo mejores perspectivas, como vos, señora Moore, podéis haberlas tenido: la relicta del coronel Sinclair. Vos, señora Moore, quizá conocierais al coronel Sinclair: tuvo alojamientos en Hampstead.»

And yet it is very probable that minute inquiries will be made; and this is what renders precaution necessary. For Mr James Harlowe will not believe that you are married; and is sure, he says, that you both lived together when Mr Hickman's application was made to Mr John Harlowe: and if you lived together any time unmarried, he infers from your character, Mr Lovelace, that it is not probable that you would ever marry. And he leaves it to his two uncles to decide, if you even should be married, whether there be not room to believe that his sister was first dishonoured; and if so, to judge of the title she will have to their favour, or to the forgiveness of any of her family. I believe, sir, this part of my letter had best to be kept from the lady.

Había oído el nombre.

What makes young Mr Harlowe the more earnest to find this out---and find it out he is resolved, and to come at his sister's speech too; and for that purpose sets out tomorrow, as I am well-informed, with a large attendance, armed, and Mr Solmes is to be of the party---is this: Mr John Harlowe has told the whole family that he will alter and new-settle his will. Mr Antony Harlowe is resolved to do the same by his; for, it seems, he has now given over all thoughts of changing his condition; having lately been disappointed in a view he had of that sort with Mrs Howe. These two brothers generally act in concert; and Mr James Harlowe dreads, and let me tell you that he has reason for it, on my Mr Harlowe's account, that his younger sister will be at last more benefited than he wishes for, by the alteration intended. He has already been endeavouring to sound his uncle Harlowe on this subject; and wanted to know whether any new application had been made to him on his sister's part. Mr Harlowe avoided a direct answer, and expressed his wishes for a general reconciliation, and his hopes that his niece was married. This offended the furious young man, and he reminded his uncle of engagements they had all entered into at his sister's going away, not to be reconciled but by general consent.

«¡Oh! Estaba emparentado con las mejores familias de Escocia; y no ha de reflexionarse sobre su viuda porque alquile alojamientos, ya lo sabéis, señora Moore; ya lo sabéis, señorita Rawlins.»

Mr John Harlowe complains to me often of the uncontrollableness of his nephew; and says that now that the young man has not anybody of whose superior sense he stands in awe, he observes not decency in his behaviour to any of them. And this makes my Mr Harlowe still more desirous than ever of bringing his younger niece into favour again. I will not say all I might of this young man's extraordinary rapaciousness---but one would think that these grasping men expect to live for ever!

Muy cierto, y muy cierto; y habían de decir por fuerza que no parecía tan lindo en dama como mi esposa ser tan censoria.

'I took the liberty but within these two hours to propose to set on foot, and offered my cover, to a correspondence between my friend, and his daughter-niece, as he still sometimes fondly calls her. She was mistress of so much prudence, I said, that I was sure she could better direct everything to its desirable end than anybody else could. But he said, he did not think himself entirely at liberty to take such a step at present; and that it was best that he should have it in his power to say, occasionally, that he had not any correspondence with her, or letter from her.

Un fundamento aquí, pensé, para procurar el auxilio de estas mujeres a fin de recobrar a la fugitiva, o al menos su connivencia en que yo lo hiciera; así como para anticiparme a cualquier futura información de la señorita Howe.

'You will see, sir, from all this, the necessity of keeping our treaty an absolute secret; and if the lady has mentioned it to her worthy friend Miss Howe, I hope it is in confidence.'

Les di un carácter de aquella virago, e insinué «que, por cabeza para tramar daño y corazón para ejecutarlo, apenas tenía igual en su sexo».

(And now, sir, a few lines in answer to yours of Monday last.)

A esta señorita Howe era, dijo la señora Moore que suponía, a quien mi esposa estaba tan deseosa de despachar un hombre y un caballo, al romper el día, con una carta que escribió antes de acostarse anoche; proponiéndose no quedarse más que hasta recibir respuesta a ella.

(Mr Harlowe was very well pleased with your readiness to come into his proposal. But as to what you both desire, that he will be present at the ceremony, he said that his nephew watched all his steps so narrowly, that he thought it was not practicable, if he were inclinable, to oblige you: but that he consented with all his heart that I should be the person privately present at the ceremony, on his part.)

La misma, dije. Sabía que recurriría en seguida a ella. Demasiado feliz habría sido si hubiera podido impedir que tal carta pasara.

(However, I think I have an expedient for this, if your lady continues to be very desirous of her uncle's presence, except he should be more determined than his answer seemed to import; of which I shall acquaint you, and perhaps of what he says to it, when I have the pleasure to see you in town. But, indeed, I think you have no time to lose. Mr Harlowe is impatient to hear that you are actually one; and I hope I may carry him down word, when I leave you next, that I saw the ceremony performed.)

O si hubiera podido manejarlo de suerte que se pusiera en manos de la señora Howe en lugar de las de su hija. Las mujeres que han vivido algún tiempo en el mundo saben mejor que alentar tales travesuras de potranca en las jóvenes esposas.

(If any obstacle arises from the lady, from you it cannot, I shall be tempted to think a little hardly of her punctilio.)

Déjame detenerme sólo a decirte, mientras lo tengo en la cabeza, que después he dado a Will su consigna para que averigüe dónde vive el hombre que ha ido con la carta de la bella fugitiva, y, si es posible, para verle a su vuelta antes de que él la vea a ella.

Mr Harlowe hopes, sir, that you will rather take pains to avoid, than to meet, this violent young man. He has the better opinion of you, let me tell you, sir, from the account I gave him of your moderation and politeness; neither of which are qualities with his nephew. But we have all of us something to amend.
